sections.heading: Architecture Overview
content: This setup runs a fully autonomous multi-agent software development pipeline across two physical machines in a home lab. Three AI agents — Product Manager, Engineering Agent, and DevOps Agent — communicate asynchronously via a self-hosted Forgejo instance to triage issues, write code, review pull requests, run quality checks, and deploy to staging.

The agents run as Linux users on a VM called Lion's Rest Inn, hosted on the Canterbury Unraid server. Each agent has its own Forgejo user identity, Hermes profile, OpenRouter API key, SSH key, and GPG signing key. They are fully independent and communicate only through Forgejo issues, PRs, and reviews — no SSH, no file handoffs, no direct API calls between agents.
Traffic flow: Stakeholder → Telegram or SSH CLI → PM Agent → Forgejo issues → Engineering Agent → Pull Requests → PM Review → DevOps Pipeline → Staging Deploy → Stakeholder merges.

The git host is Forgejo (git.chrisharrsch.com) running as a Docker container on Canterbury with a PostgreSQL backend, fronted by Nginx Proxy Manager. The previous GitHub org was replaced by Forgejo after GitHub's machine-account ToS limits capped the number of agent identities on a free plan — self-hosting removes the limit entirely. The full Forgejo deployment process is documented in the Self-Hosted Git with Forgejo guide.

Stack: Three Hermes Agent v0.19.0 instances (uv tool install, no venvs), each with its own model and budget, running on Ubuntu 24.04 with Docker for staging deployments. All LLM calls go through OpenRouter.

sections.heading: Agent Setup Pattern
sections.subtitle: Every agent follows this identical bootstrap procedure. Captured as a reusable skill in the agent-onboarding skill in the skill library.
steps: Create Linux user on the Agent VM with Docker group access
Generate SSH key and GPG signing key (ed25519)
Create Forgejo user account with plus-addressed email (harrsch.agents+<agent>@gmail.com)
Upload SSH public key + GPG public key, add to Harrsch-Industries org under the agents team
Generate a Forgejo PAT (scopes: write:repository, write:issue, read:user, read:admin)
Install Hermes via uv tool install hermes-agent --python python3 (never a local venv)
Write config.yaml with model, provider, and persona system prompt
Wire PAT via tea login add and register the git credential helper (tea login helper setup), deploy the forgejo-api wrapper script
Create cron jobs with --workdir /home/<agent> to avoid .git permission errors

sections.heading: PR Review Workflow
sections.subtitle: A three-tier review system that ties all agents together. Saved as a reusable skill in the skill library.
content: When the Engineering Agent opens a PR, it labels it pm-review (default) or auto-approve (mechanical changes only). The PM Agent polls every 10 minutes for unreviewed PRs and applies the tier matrix:
Tier 1 — Auto-Approve (auto-approve label): For dependency bumps, CI config changes, minor docs, pure refactors. PM sanity-checks then squash-merges automatically. No human involvement.

Tier 2 — PM Review + Ping (pm-review label, default): PM reviews the diff for hardcoded secrets, injection vectors, missing auth, debug code, missing tests, logic errors, and breaking API changes. If clean: approves (does not merge) and sends a Telegram notification to the stakeholder with a summary.
Tier 3 — Escalate (human-review label or critical findings): PM flags the stakeholder immediately on Telegram.

If PM finds issues in Tier 2, they submit a formal Forgejo review requesting changes. The Engineering Agent detects this on its next poll cycle, reads the review comments, fixes the code, pushes, and re-requests review from the PM.
After the PM approves, the DevOps Agent runs a 4-stage pipeline. If all stages pass, it also approves. The PR then sits with two approvals waiting for the stakeholder's final review and merge.

sections.heading: DevOps Pipeline Stages
content: The DevOps Agent runs this pipeline on every new or updated PR that passes PM review:
1. Code Quality — Linting (ruff for Python, ESLint for JS), type checking (mypy), security scan (bandit), secrets detection. All stage failures block the pipeline.
2. Build & Tests — Install dependencies, run unit tests (pytest, npm test), check coverage. All tests must pass.
3. Staging Deploy — Docker Compose build and deploy to /home/staging/, verify healthcheck endpoint, run integration tests. Stacks are isolated by project and PR number.
4. Cleanup & Report — Tear down the staging stack, post a PR comment with per-stage pass/fail results. If all pass: approve the PR. If any fail: request changes with details.

The Security Bot then performs a separate deep-dive audit on the final code and staging deployment — static analysis (OWASP Top 10, dependency CVEs, secret detection) plus dynamic checks on the running instance. Critical findings block the merge; lower-severity findings are filed as recommendations.
A Docker Compose staging template is at /home/staging/templates/. Forgejo Actions (a GitHub Actions-compatible CI system) is available on the instance for future pipeline automation.
Future goal: deploy containers directly to the Canterbury bare-metal host, currently blocked by incomplete Docker TLS configuration on Unraid.

sections.heading: Agent Communication
content: All inter-agent communication happens through Forgejo. No agent ever SSHes into another or reads another agent's files. This eliminates coupling between agent runtimes and keeps a full audit trail on the Forgejo instance.
PM → Eng: Creates issues with requirements, assigns to the engineering agent's Forgejo user. Picked up on the next poll cycle.
Eng → PM: Opens PRs with labels. Comments on issues with status updates. Re-requests review after addressing feedback.
PM → Stakeholder: Telegram notifications for PRs ready for review, escalations, and status summaries.
DevOps → PRs: Pipeline reports as PR comments. Approves or requests changes based on pipeline outcome.
Maximum delay between any action and its downstream processing is 10 minutes (the cron interval), which is fast enough for a home lab.

sections.heading: Skills & Knowledge Base
content: All reusable agent workflows are saved as Hermes skills (markdown files with YAML frontmatter that agents can load as procedural memory):

agent-onboarding — Full bootstrap procedure: Linux user, SSH/GPG keys, Hermes install, config, git setup, Forgejo PAT wiring, cron creation. Includes email convention, PATH pitfalls, and gateway setup.
pr-review-workflow — Three-tier PR approval system. Covers the decision matrix, tea CLI commands for each tier, and the agent feedback loop.
Both skills live at Harrsch-Industries/skill-library under devops/<skill>/SKILL.md.
A master configuration reference (AGENTS.md) tracks every agent's specific SSH key fingerprint, GPG key ID, model, budget, cron job ID, and Forgejo PAT for maintenance.

sections.heading: Cost Notes
content: All agents use OpenRouter with independent daily budget caps. No keys are shared.

The PM and DevOps agents use a cost-effective model since most of their work is executing terminal commands (git, tea, docker) rather than heavy reasoning. The Engineering Agent gets a stronger, more expensive model and the largest budget since it does the actual coding.
Each cron runs every 10 minutes. When there's nothing new to process, the cron responds with '[SILENT]' and skips inference, keeping costs negligible during idle periods.
